source.title_on_document: GenAI and Search Tools in Design Education: Comparative Analysis of Student Creativity, Outcomes, and Experiences

paper_design_summary: 45 undergraduate industrial design students were randomly assigned, 15 per group, to design a cognitive training wooden toy for older adults in 160 minutes with no external tool, with Pinterest image search, or with Midjourney image generation. Ten expert evaluators, blind to group, rated each A3 sketch on effectiveness, originality, usability, and feasibility on five-point scales. Quantitative results are shown as a bar chart of group scores (statistic not named) without value labels (Figure 3); the paper names Friedman tests but prints no test statistics, standard deviations, or p-values.

studies.label: Design ideation experiment (no tool vs Pinterest vs Midjourney)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Tool condition for the design task: no external tool (G1), Pinterest image search (G2), or Midjourney generative AI (G3)
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three experimental conditions, with 15 students in each group.

arms.name: G1 no tool
arms.description: Control group; not permitted to use any external tools for searching or generating visual materials

arms.name: G2 Pinterest
arms.description: Restricted to Pinterest as an image search tool; short standardized training; kept a log of search keywords and reference images

arms.name: G3 Midjourney
arms.description: Restricted to Midjourney as a generative AI tool for image creation; short standardized training; documented prompts and generated outputs

participants.exclusions: None reported. Figure 1 says 45 students engaged in the design task, and the ten experts 'independently evaluated all sketches' (PDF p. 5, printed p. 145). The analyzed count of 45 (15 per arm) rests on these statements; the paper does not give a separate analyzed count.
participants.who: Undergraduate students majoring in industrial design at one university (14 females, 31 males)
participants.quote: This study recruited 45 undergraduate students majoring in industrial design from a university (N = 45; 14 females, 31 males).
participants.locator: PDF p. 3 (printed p. 143), Methods; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 144), Figure 1

ai_tool.how_used: G3 students used Midjourney to generate images during ideation, after a short standardized training, and documented prompts and generated outputs; researchers monitored compliance on site. The final scored output was a hand-drawn A3 marker sketch.

task.description: Design a cognitive training wooden toy for older adults; each student produced an A3 marker sketch with annotations describing the concept, interaction logic, and usage scenario

outcomes.name: Originality (expert rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Ten experts with industrial design experience, blind to group assignment, rated each sketch on a five-point scale; descriptive statistics and Friedman tests (SPSS 30). The paper does not state the unit of the Friedman tests; Figure 3 is a bar chart of group scores (statistic not named) without value labels.

contrasts.reported: Text: 'with G3 achieving the highest originality but the lowest usability and feasibility'. Figure 3 shows G3 above G2 on originality. Bars have no numeric value labels; no SDs, test statistics, or p-values printed.

eligibility.reason: Randomized experiment (paper states random assignment, 15 per group) with 45 students across all three arms, below the 50-person threshold (PDF p. 3, printed p. 143). Expert-rated originality, effectiveness, usability, and feasibility are scored on the output. Listed in the screening report as a small randomized experiment. The homogenization and imitation risks in the abstract come from qualitative process and interview analysis; no diversity measure across people is computed.

one_line_finding: With 15 students per arm, blind expert ratings put the Midjourney group highest on originality and above the no-tool group on effectiveness, but lowest on usability and feasibility; quantitative results appear as a bar chart of group scores (statistic not named) without value labels or reported test statistics (PDF pp. 5-6, Figure 3).
